title: Form controls alternative
body:
I'd like to point out a missing feature in the native "required" control validation.
Suppose I have a form in which I ask users to input either email or telephone number for contact, both are appreciated too, but at least one MUST be given. This means I want the form to stop submission if neither email nor phone number are provided.
I can do it in several ways, of course, but each of them loses something:
1. I can use a single "text" control with a pattern allowing an email or a phone number to be inserted. But this means that I cannot rely upon autocompletion, and I also have to write regex for email and phone numbers.
2. I can discard "required" attribute altogether and configure a custom invalidity message. This means relying upon a non-native script mechanism (and also having to write more verbose and more difficult instructions, apart from localisation issues)
3. I can play with "disabled" attribute, which allows required form controls not to be filled in, but again this relies upon non-native script solutions and it needs a mechanism for detecting which control is going to be filled in (e.g. a series of radio buttons: "How would you prefer being contacted? ()phone ()email ()both

I would suggest you 2 ways to allow a half-native approach to alternative controls:
1. extend to every form control the mechanism for radio buttons, so that controls with the same name don't suffer from being missing if at least one of them is compiled (of course a name in the form of name="foo[]" would allow the server to process more than one value associated with the same name). This would be especially useful with series of homogeneous controls (e.g. a series of checkbox inputs where at least one must be chosen)
2. avoid constraint validation for not rendered controls, or at least for controls with the "hidden" attribute, unless the rendering state is overridden via CSS. This would allow a two-step solution as defined previously (n.3), with the difference that CSS is less non-native, especially if specified with an HTML attribute. Consider that, if a required control is erroneously hidden, then the form "freezes" and the user cannot even understand why data aren't sent.
